title: Optimal logarithmic-label regret for online two-local learning
formal:
Assume the planted-clique detection hypothesis stated below. Do there exist positive integers \(C,a\) and one uniform classical randomized learner such that, for every \(n,k\ge2\), \(T,b\ge1\), and every sequence of two-local prediction rounds on \(n\) items and \(k\) labels, the learner uses at most \(C(n+k+T+b+2)^a\) bit operations per round and has expected regret at most
\[
C\sqrt{n\log_2(k)\,T}?
\]
The learner must work for every fixed sequence of item pairs and rational payoff tables as defined below. This historical target has a negative answer under the stated hypothesis.
why: Local predictions can be easier than recovering a global assignment, but this result identifies a computational price for a growing label set even with full feedback. It connects efficient online prediction with detecting hidden combinatorial structure in random graphs.
status_note: Conditionally resolved negatively by the COLT 2015 label-dependent hardness result, assuming planted-clique detection below the square-root scale is hard. The selected target is the first, two-local question from COLT 2014. The second higher-locality question is not declared resolved. Source and scope review completed on 18 September 2026; no independent full-proof or Lean audit is claimed.

progress.text: The source asks separately for optimal two-local regret and for improvements for larger local subsets.

The label-dependent computational lower bound rules out the first target under the planted-clique detection conjecture. It is a conditional result, not an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound.

sentences: In each round a learner labels a presented pair of items before seeing their payoff table.
Its benchmark is the best fixed labeling of all items in hindsight.
The historical question asks for polynomial computation and regret proportional to the square root of n log(k) T.
A 2015 reduction rules this out under a planted-clique detection hypothesis.
The card archives that conditional two-local result and does not close the separate question about larger local subsets.

definitions:
Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The universe of items is \([n]\), and labels belong to \([k]\). Before play begins, an adversary fixes a sequence \((i_t,j_t,p_t)_{t=1}^T\), where \(1\le i_t<j_t\le n\) and \(p_t:[k]^2\to[-1,1]\cap\mathbb Q\) is a complete rational payoff table. Each entry is given by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with total encoding length at most \(b\). The fixed sequence is hidden from the learner and independent of its coins. The learner knows \(n,k,T,b\).

In round \(t\), the pair \((i_t,j_t)\) is revealed. Based on this pair, the parameters, all preceding feedback and fresh private fair random bits, the learner chooses labels \((a_t,b_t)\in[k]^2\). Then the entire table \(p_t\) is revealed and the learner earns \(p_t(a_t,b_t)\). The symbol \(b_t\) denotes a label and is unrelated to the precision parameter \(b\). The learner need not maintain a consistent global labeling across different rounds. In particular it may make local randomized predictions that could not arise from a fixed global assignment.

The benchmark is the best single labeling \(\ell:[n]\to[k]\) in hindsight. Expected regret, in units of total payoff, is
\[
\max_{\ell:[n]\to[k]}\sum_{t=1}^T p_t(\ell(i_t),\ell(j_t))-
\mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^T p_t(a_t,b_t)\right].
\]
Expectation is over the learner's randomness for each fixed sequence. Feedback is the full table, not only the chosen pair's reward. The performance guarantee is uniform over variable label counts; allowing a constant to depend on \(k\) would change the question. The selected model uses an oblivious adversary, which is already sufficient for the cited impossibility result.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine. Initialization is included in the first round's bound. The bound holds on every execution and includes all input and table access, arithmetic, random-bit generation, memory operations and label output. The exponent and coefficient are independent of \(n,k,T,b\). No advice, exact-real operation or computational oracle is supplied. The regret bound has no hidden dependence on payoff precision.

For the planted-clique hypothesis, let \(G(N,1/2)\) be a simple undirected graph on \([N]\), each unordered pair independently present with probability \(1/2\). Let \(G(N,1/2,q)\) be obtained by first generating this graph, then selecting an independent uniformly random \(q\)-element vertex set and adding all missing edges inside it. The hypothesis says that, for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), there is no uniform classical randomized algorithm of worst-case polynomial bit time in \(N\) which, for all sufficiently large \(N\), distinguishes these two distributions with \(q=\lfloor N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\): its probability of answering random on \(G(N,1/2)\) and its probability of answering planted on \(G(N,1/2,q)\) must each be at least \(4/5\). Each probability includes the graph generation and the algorithm's coins. The graph is given by its full adjacency matrix. The algorithm and its polynomial bound may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\); the hypothesis excludes them for every such \(\varepsilon\).

The assumption is an average-case computational hypothesis, not the assertion \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The card selects the first question in the original source, concerning pairs and logarithmic dependence on the number of labels. It does not close the separate question about local subsets of more than two items.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated learner-existence proposition under the precise planted-clique hypothesis. A negative answer must address the uniform logarithmic-label regret guarantee, not just one restricted learning method. The known conditional negative result warrants historical archival; no Lean formalization is claimed complete.

source_formulation.text: The source poses two separate questions. This card selects its first: efficient two-local learning with regret of order sqrt(n log(k) T), and records its known conditional negative resolution. The finite rational, oblivious-sequence model is already covered by the later binary-payoff reduction. Selection of this branch and archival are the announced editorial default after an unanswered optional question.
source_formulation.caption: Christiano 2014 §2, first bullet; Awasthi–Charikar–Lai–Risteski 2015 §2.1 and Corollary 1.

context_blocks.text: A fixed global labeling is the comparator, but the learner only needs to predict labels for the presented pair. This separates local prediction from the generally hard problem of finding the best global explanation.

The 2015 work improves the efficient upper bound to order sqrt(n k T) and derives planted-clique hardness for a fixed polynomial improvement in the label dependence. The logarithmic-label target is below that conditional barrier.

The hardness reduction presents pairs of vertex clusters and reveals binary adjacency payoff tables. Consequently, the conditional obstruction persists for finite-bit full-information feedback and fixed, rather than reactive, sequences.
